title: Vision
text:
Ecologists routinely investigate why populations change, species interact, communities assemble, and ecosystems respond to disturbance. Their studies contribute observations, experiments, statistical estimates, predictions, and explanations. But synthesizing these contributions as causal knowledge is more demanding than collecting the relationships they report.
Studies can examine similarly named variables yet address different interventions, outcomes, populations, timescales, or causal pathways. Even when authors use comparable causal language, the assumptions supporting their interpretations may differ. An apparent consensus in reported associations need not constitute agreement about an identifiable causal effect.

title: Vision
section: A missing dimension in the literature
text:
A missing dimension in the literature
Conventional reviews and literature-mining systems are valuable for organizing topics, methods, variables, and conclusions. The Causal Atlas of Ecology asks what additional understanding becomes possible when we also attend to the causal question a study poses, the assumptions its inference requires, and the evidence it provides.
This is not a claim that existing ecological studies lack value. Rather, it is an invitation to examine more carefully which kinds of knowledge each study contributes, where uncertainty remains, and when findings are meaningfully comparable.

title: Vision
text:
Our long-term vision
The program aims to develop systematic, reproducible approaches for interpreting and evaluating causal knowledge in published ecological research. Over time, validated methods could support structured representations of causal questions, assumptions, and evidence, enabling new kinds of comparison and synthesis across studies.




Three-stage conceptual vision: published research, reconstruction and evaluation, structured causal knowledge.



Long-term research vision. The diagram illustrates conceptual stages, not an implemented end-to-end system.

title: Vision
text:
Why begin with ecology?
Ecological systems are complex, interconnected, and dynamic. Their study combines experiments, observations, longitudinal measurements, comparative designs, and models across scales. Ecologists also confront familiar inferential challenges: confounding, feedback, imperfect measurement, selection, and context-dependent effects.
These characteristics make ecology an especially informative setting for investigating the relationship between scientific questions, causal assumptions, analytical decisions, and conclusions.

title: Vision
text:
Potential beyond ecology
Although ecology is the program’s initial focus, the underlying questions are relevant to many disciplines that attempt to infer causes from heterogeneous bodies of evidence. Any extension beyond ecology would require domain-specific evaluation, methodological adaptation, and independent validation.

Scope note. The Atlas is a research program, not presently a complete database of ecological causal relationships. Its long-term form will depend on what the development and validation phases establish.

title: Are we answering the question we asked?
text: A study can fit a sophisticated statistical model, obtain precise coefficients, and still leave its central scientific question unresolved. The issue is not necessarily poor modeling. It may be a mismatch between the question that motivated the work and the quantity the analysis actually estimates.

title: Are we answering the question we asked?
text:
From question to target
Suppose an ecologist asks about the total effect of canopy cover on bird abundance. That question differs from asking about a direct effect that excludes changes through food resources, or about the association between canopy cover and bird counts among otherwise similar sampled sites. Each quantity can be scientifically useful, but they are not interchangeable.
A target causal quantity, or estimand, clarifies what is being compared. A causal model can then help identify the assumptions needed to connect the target to observed data. Only after that step does it make sense to debate an estimator, functional form, or model-fitting procedure.

title: Are we answering the question we asked?
text:
Models are tools, not questions
Generalized linear models, mixed models, additive models, and structural equation models can each serve important roles. None independently defines the scientific effect of interest. Adding covariates, selecting paths, or optimizing fit cannot substitute for deciding which effect the study intends to learn.
The practical lesson is not to abandon familiar models. It is to organize their use around clearly specified questions and assumptions.

title: Are we answering the question we asked?
text:
A question for readers
Could two analysts fit the same dataset successfully while answering different causal questions? If so, what would you need to specify before deciding which result is relevant?
Return to Perspectives

title: Causal language is not causal identification
text: Ecologists often write that one factor drives, determines, shapes, or influences another. These words can express a scientific hypothesis, summarize a proposed mechanism, or interpret an empirical result. But their causal force does not, by itself, establish that the study design and analysis identify the effect being discussed.

title: Causal language is not causal identification
text:
A distinction worth preserving
Consider a study reporting that forest cover is associated with bird abundance. A causal question might ask how bird abundance would change if forest cover were altered, holding relevant background conditions appropriately in view. That intervention-oriented question is not answered merely by finding a statistical association. It also requires assumptions about possible common causes, measurement, selection, and the temporal organization of the system.
A paper may be careful in its methods but expansive in its discussion. Another may pose a causal question in its introduction yet report only predictive performance. Neither pattern can be judged adequately by counting a few words in isolation. The scientific meaning depends on the relationship among the question, evidence, analysis, and interpretation.

title: Causal language is not causal identification
text:
Why it matters for synthesis
If a review treats every causal-sounding statement as an identified causal finding, it risks combining conclusions that have different evidentiary status. Conversely, treating all observational findings as merely descriptive can obscure important design-based causal work. A more useful approach is to evaluate the claims and their inferential support separately.
The Causal Atlas of Ecology investigates how such distinctions can be made systematically across scientific literature. That remains a research question, not a completed census of ecological practice.

title: Causal language is not causal identification
text:
A question for readers
When you read that a variable affects an outcome, can you identify the intervention, comparison, population, and assumptions that give that statement its causal meaning?
Return to Perspectives

title: The Team
text:
Principal Investigator | Behavioral Complexity and Causality Lab | University of Wyoming
Patrick Kelley is an ecologist whose work connects tropical field research, animal behavior, complex systems, artificial intelligence, and causal inference. With more than 25 years of research experience, he leads the Behavioral Complexity and Causality Lab at the University of Wyoming. His research spans bird–plant interactions in Hawaiʻi, nest predation and animal communication in Panama, and the development of novel sensors and electronic instrumentation for quantifying animal behavior. Beyond ecology, he has contributed to the development and evaluation of large language models (LLMs) through professional work in AI training, scientific reasoning, and model assessment. His interdisciplinary research also extends to heritage paper science, where he applies structural causal models and experimental approaches to investigate the mechanisms of paper degradation, preservation, and conservation treatments. Across these efforts, he explores how both existing LLMs and specialized, locally trained AI models can support scientific discovery and evidence synthesis. Through the Causal Atlas of Ecology, his lab is developing computational approaches to extracting and organizing causal knowledge from the scientific literature while examining how scientific questions, study designs, and analytical methods support—or undermine—valid scientific inference.

title: Development
text: The Causal Atlas of Ecology is being developed through a phased research program combining causal inference, artificial intelligence, and systematic analysis of scientific literature. The roadmap below describes the intended progression of work, from conceptual foundations and computational methods to human validation and broader synthesis. Methods and priorities may evolve in response to empirical evaluation, expert review, and available resources.

title: Development
text:
Research roadmap


Phase I | Foundational research


Conceptual foundations
The goal of Phase I is to establish a framework for interpreting causal information in scientific publications, including distinctions among causal questions, scientific claims, assumptions, estimands, and causal identification. We aim to develop definitions and classification criteria for causal, associational, predictive, and descriptive statements.
Intended output: A scientifically grounded conceptual framework and standardized criteria for interpreting causal claims in the ecological literature.




Phase II | Computational methods


AI-assisted extraction and annotation
The goal of Phase II is to develop LLM-based agent workflows to extract and classify scientific claims from ecological literature. Our specific aim is to establish standardized annotation protocols and a web-based platform for independent human evaluation of AI-generated classifications.
Intended output: A reproducible AI-assisted extraction pipeline, a structured preliminary corpus of scientific claims, and protocols for human annotation and evaluation.




Phase III | Human validation


Reliability, agreement, and model evaluation
The goal of Phase III is to evaluate the AI-generated classifications against independent annotations by trained graduate researchers. Multiple human annotators will assess overlapping sets of scientific statements, allowing the project to quantify agreement among human raters and compare AI performance (of multiple LLMs) to that of human annotators.
Intended output: A human-annotated reference dataset, quantitative assessments of inter-rater reliability and AI performance, and evidence-based refinements to the extraction and classification methods.




Phase IV | Broader analysis


Expansion across ecological literature
The goal of Phase IV is to apply our validated computational methods to a more diverse set of ecological publications. We aim to examine how causal claims, relationships, and forms of scientific evidence vary across research disciplines, study designs, years, and analytical approaches. This will allow us to reconstruct structured causal relationships and evaluate the assumptions underlying scientific conclusions.
Intended output: An expanded corpus of ecological causal claims, comparative analyses of scientific reasoning and evidence, and research manuscripts supported by validated methods.




Phase V | Public research products


Atlas construction and dissemination
The goal of Phase V is to develop accessible research products that organize and communicate causal knowledge extracted from the ecological literature. Potential outputs include structured datasets, searchable causal relationships, documented computational methods, and tools supporting scientific evidence synthesis and causal reasoning. Our aim is to streamline hypothesis discovery and improve integration of causal dependencies into ecological modeling.
Intended output: Public research resources, datasets, and publications whose scope and reliability are supported by prior evaluation.



Development status (November 2026). Current work of this project is on Phases I and II, centering on developing the computational and human-annotation infrastructure. Foundational research and computational methods development are underway. Initial AI-assisted extraction workflows and human-annotation infrastructure are being developed in preparation for evaluation in Spring 2027.

title: Development
text:
Current focus
The program’s initial emphasis is on conceptual development and systematic approaches to evaluating published ecological studies. Protocol refinement and pilot evaluation are part of this early work. The descriptions here are deliberately qualitative; quantitative results will be reported only when appropriately checked and ready for dissemination.

Development status (October 2026). Early-stage research and methods development. The phases above are a roadmap, not a statement that all stages have started. No comprehensive public Atlas or production-scale analysis is claimed.

title: Causal Atlas of Ecology
text:
A research venture of the Behavioral Complexity and Causality Lab · University of Wyoming




Mapping the causal knowledge embedded in ecological science.

Ecology has produced an extraordinary body of research investigating why natural systems behave as they do. Yet the causal knowledge contained in this literature remains difficult to evaluate, compare, and synthesize. Studies may share variables and terminology while asking different questions, invoking different assumptions, and supporting different inferences.
The Causal Atlas of Ecology is a developing research program investigating how ecological studies formulate causal questions, support their claims, and contribute to an accumulating body of causal knowledge.
The Causal Atlas of Ecology is a research program within the Behavioral Complexity and Causality Lab at the University of Wyoming. The program connects ecological research, causal inference, scientific knowledge synthesis, and computational methods.

title: Causal Atlas of Ecology
text:
The scientific challenge
A statistical relationship is not automatically an answer to a causal question. Nor do two reported effects necessarily describe the same causal quantity. Meaningful synthesis requires attention to what was asked, what was measured, what assumptions were made, and what the evidence can support.
The Atlas seeks to make these distinctions more explicit and, over time, more systematically examinable across the ecological literature.




Conceptual relationship among scientific questions, causal assumptions, evidence, and synthesis.



Conceptual framework: causal knowledge synthesis depends on interpreting questions, assumptions, and evidence together. This is a research vision, not a depiction of an operational atlas.

title: Causal Atlas of Ecology
text:
A program under development
Initial work focuses on conceptual foundations, systematic evaluation of scientific literature, and approaches for reconstructing and assessing causal claims. The long-term ambition is to develop validated methods that can support broader analysis and synthesis across ecological research.

Project status. The Causal Atlas of Ecology is in an early research and methods-development stage. A comprehensive public atlas, validated large-scale dataset, and production search interface have not yet been launched. See Development for the proposed research phases.

title: When evidence accumulates, does knowledge?
text: A growing literature can make a scientific topic appear well understood. Many studies may report effects involving the same variables, and a synthesis may combine their estimates into a compelling summary. Yet an important question remains: are the studies estimating the same thing?

title: When evidence accumulates, does knowledge?
text:
The challenge of comparability
Two studies may both examine how habitat disturbance relates to biodiversity, while differing in exposure definition, temporal scale, sampled populations, confounding structure, and treatment of intermediate variables. A coefficient from one analysis may represent a conditional association; another may approximate a total causal effect under explicit assumptions. Averaging them does not automatically create a meaningful causal summary.
This is not an argument against meta-analysis or evidence synthesis. It is an argument for making the inferential target and supporting assumptions part of the synthesis itself.

title: When evidence accumulates, does knowledge?
text:
Toward structured causal evidence
A richer account of scientific knowledge would describe not only which variables appear together in the literature, but also the questions researchers asked, the assumptions they relied upon, and the limits of what their designs could identify. Such structure might help reveal areas of agreement, unresolved ambiguity, and opportunities for stronger research designs.
Developing and evaluating methods for that kind of synthesis is a long-term objective of the Causal Atlas of Ecology. Its feasibility and limitations must be established through research rather than presumed in advance.

title: When evidence accumulates, does knowledge?
text:
A question for readers
Before pooling reported effects, can you explain why they represent comparable causal quantities?

title: Research Framework
text:
Ecologists routinely investigate why populations change, species interact, communities assemble, and ecosystems respond to disturbance. Their studies contribute observations, experiments, statistical estimates, predictions, and explanations. Yet synthesizing these contributions as causal knowledge requires more than collecting the relationships they report.
Studies may examine similarly named variables while addressing different interventions, outcomes, populations, timescales, or causal pathways. Even when authors use comparable causal language, the assumptions supporting their interpretations may differ. An apparent consensus in reported associations does not necessarily constitute agreement about an identifiable causal effect.
Conventional reviews and literature-mining systems are valuable for organizing topics, methods, variables, and conclusions. The Causal Atlas of Ecology investigates what additional understanding becomes possible when we systematically examine the causal questions studies pose, the assumptions their inferences require, and the evidence they provide.

title: Research Framework
text:
01 | Causal language and scientific claims
How do ecological papers express questions about causes, effects, and mechanisms? How does the language motivating a study compare with its description of methods and interpretation of results?
This theme examines the relationship between what a paper appears to ask and what its authors claim to have learned. It recognizes that descriptive, associational, predictive, and causal statements serve different scientific purposes.
Computational approaches, including LLM-assisted extraction and classification, offer opportunities to investigate these distinctions systematically. Independent human annotation and validation are essential for evaluating their reliability.

title: Research Framework
text:
02 | Causal identification
Under what conditions do study designs and analytical choices support the causal effects being discussed? Which assumptions are stated, which remain implicit, and which may be difficult to assess from a published account?
Causal identification concerns whether a target causal quantity can, in principle, be learned from available evidence under specified assumptions. It is distinct from selecting a statistical model, estimating parameters, or achieving high predictive accuracy.




A stylized causal diagram showing a common cause, exposure, mediator, and outcome.



Illustrative causal structure. Arrows represent hypothesized causal relationships, not relationships established by data. Different causal questions may require different treatment of the same variables.

title: Research Framework
text:
03 | Causal reconstruction
Can scientific questions, proposed causal structures, and relevant inferential assumptions be reconstructed systematically from published research? How should ambiguity, missing information, and competing interpretations be represented?
This theme investigates the potential and limitations of computational assistance in reconstructing causal models from scientific literature. A reconstructed causal diagram represents an interpretation of reported evidence and assumptions, not independent proof of the underlying causal structure.

title: Research Framework
text:
04 | Causal knowledge synthesis
When do results from separate studies address comparable causal quantities? How can differences in context, measurement, population, intervention, and assumptions be made visible during synthesis?
The long-term aim is to move beyond aggregating reported relationships, some of which may be spurious or causally misleading, toward evaluating which bodies of evidence can support particular causal questions.
This approach could reveal where independent studies provide convergent causal evidence, where apparent agreement conceals incompatible assumptions, and where important gaps in causal understanding remain.

title: Research Framework
text:
Methodological commitments
The program is guided by five core principles:

Ask estimand-aware questions before building models. Define the scientific question and target causal quantity (estimand) before selecting analytical methods or interpreting model outputs.
Make causal assumptions explicit. Distinguish assumptions about the data-generating process from observed statistical associations and fitted relationships.
Establish causal identification before estimation. Determine whether a target causal effect is identifiable under the proposed assumptions before evaluating estimation methods, precision, or statistical significance.
Be transparent about uncertainty and causal ambiguity. Treat incomplete reporting, competing causal explanations, and unresolved assumptions as substantive limitations rather than details to be overlooked.
Prioritize transparency, reproducibility, and validation. Document computational procedures, evaluate AI-generated classifications against independent human judgments, and subject methodological conclusions to critical scrutiny.

title: Research
section: What this page does not claim
text:
What this page does not claim
These themes describe an active research agenda. They do not imply that all four lines of inquiry have been completed, that automated reconstruction is fully validated, or that the Atlas currently contains a comprehensive body of identified causal effects.

title: People
text:
Data infrastructure

Kamryn Crozier
Originally from Cheyenne, Wyoming, Kamryn is an undergraduate student at the University of Wyoming majoring in Physiology with a minor in Neuroscience. As a member of the Behavioral Complexity and Causality Lab, she is helping develop the computational infrastructure for the Causal Atlas of Ecology. In Spring 2027, she will help coordinate the annotation process with graduate student researchers, contributing to the development of a human-validated dataset for evaluating AI interpretations of scientific evidence. With an interest in pursuing a career in the medical field, her aims are to gain hands-on research experience and to strengthen her ability to read and critically evaluate primary scientific literature. She has a particular interest in applying the project’s methods to medical research as a complementary project. Her love of the outdoors and curiosity about how nature works bring a personal connection to her work in biological research.

title: People
text:
Data collection
In Spring 2027, five University of Wyoming graduate students will join the Causal Atlas of ECology to independently annotate scientific statements extracted from the ecological literature, identify causal relationships, and classify types of scientific claims. Their annotations will provide a human-validated reference dataset for evaluating AI-generated classifications, quantifying variability among human annotators, and improving the accuracy of automated causal knowledge extraction.

text:
Our research vision
The Causal Atlas of Ecology aims to develop systematic, reproducible approaches for interpreting, evaluating, and synthesizing causal knowledge from published ecological research.
By combining causal inference with computational methods, including large language models (LLMs) and independent human evaluation, the program seeks to examine how scientific claims are expressed, how causal conclusions are supported, and when findings across studies are meaningfully comparable.
Over time, validated methods could support structured representations of causal questions, relationships, assumptions, and evidence, enabling new forms of scientific comparison and synthesis.

Research questions

text:
Potential beyond ecology
Although ecology is the program’s initial focus, the underlying questions are relevant to other disciplines seeking to infer causes from heterogeneous bodies of evidence.
Methods developed through the Causal Atlas could eventually inform causal knowledge synthesis in environmental science, medicine, public health, and other research fields. Any extension would require domain-specific adaptation, methodological evaluation, and independent validation.
